strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear identification of key challenges (causalization and action conditioning)
Strong empirical results across diverse domains (robotics RT-1 and game simulation CS:GO) with consistent improvements over baselines
Clever mixed weight transfer scheme for temporal convolutions that preserves pre-trained information better than naive approaches
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including ablations, qualitative results, and downstream task validation (Real2Sim policy evaluation)
Systematic technical approach with clear algorithms and good reproducibility details provided
Demonstrates practical viability of adapting pre-trained video diffusion models to interactive world modeling
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: mixed weight transfer is incremental heuristic; relies heavily on existing techniques (Diffusion Forcing, causal masking, CFG); action dropout for guidance is straightforward
Severely limited experimental scope: only one base model tested (DynamiCrafter 1.1B/320×512); generalization to other video diffusion models, resolutions, or architectures unclear
Critical missing comparison: no evaluation against AVID [43], the most directly related recent work addressing the same problem
Insufficient validation of causalization claims: causal generation tested only indirectly through final video quality; no ablations removing history frames to verify predictions depend only on past
Arbitrary design choices without justification: action dropout p=0.2, guidance scale λ=2.5, rescale 0.7 appear unmotivated; mixed weight transfer initialization (mean) not compared to alternatives

Weak action conditioning evaluation: standard video metrics (FVD, SSIM) measure visual similarity not action responsiveness; no quantitative metrics for action-controlled generation quality; counterfactual reasoning only shown qualitatively
Limited downstream task evaluation: only one Real2Sim task (drawer closing) with modest sample size (N=80) and human verification; no other RL/planning tasks tested
Fairness concerns in baselines: non-autoregressive methods compared in autoregressive setting; different training setups make 7-day vs 100k-step comparison non-direct
Incomplete ablations: missing studies on action dropout probability, guidance hyperparameters, Diffusion Forcing contribution, alternative weight transfer schemes
Insufficient failure analysis: acknowledged failures (Figures 6, 10) not systematically characterized; 'regressing to familiar scenes' suggests mode collapse but prevalence/conditions unknown

strengths: Well-motivated problem of leveraging pre-trained video diffusion models for interactive world modeling with practical implications
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across two distinct domains (robotics and games) with multiple metrics and ablation studies
Strong empirical results showing significant improvements over baselines (81.8% FVD improvement on CS:GO)
Generally clear presentation with effective use of figures to illustrate the transformation pipeline
Real2Sim policy evaluation demonstrates downstream utility beyond video prediction metrics
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing Diffusion Forcing [8], standard causal masking, and a straightforward weight transfer heuristic; mixed weight transfer lacks principled justification
Unfair baseline comparisons: baselines evaluated in non-autoregressive settings while Vid2World uses autoregressive rollout; evaluation setup confounds inference procedure with method quality
Missing critical comparisons: AVID [43], a closely related work addressing similar problems, is not directly compared despite being mentioned in related work
Insufficient ablations: action dropout probability (p=0.2), guidance scale (2.5), and rescale factor (0.7) appear arbitrary with no ablation studies or sensitivity analysis

Weak validation of action conditioning: Real2Sim experiment (80 trajectories, 1 task, human evaluation) too limited to convincingly demonstrate counterfactual reasoning; no quantitative metrics for action fidelity
Unjustified design choices: why average weights for mixed transfer? Why not learn or initialize to zero? No comparison of alternatives
Limited generalization evidence: only tested on 1.1B DynamiCrafter model; authors acknowledge 'relatively lightweight'; only two domains; no evidence scalability to larger models (Sora, Veo-2)

Overclaimed contributions: abstract claims 'first to systematically explore' but heavily relies on Diffusion Forcing [8] from prior work; misleading 'causalization' framing when primary enabler is prior technique
Missing ablations: no analysis separating Diffusion Forcing's contribution from architectural changes; no ablation on action dropout types or guidance hyperparameter sensitivity
Insufficient analysis of failure cases: Figure 6 shows failures but no systematic characterization of when and why the approach fails; temporal consistency not analyzed for long horizons

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing the gap between non-interactive video diffusion models and interactive world models
Strong empirical results across domains (81.8% FVD improvement on CS:GO, significant gains on RT-1)
Technically sound approach combining diffusion forcing, causal architectures, and classifier-free guidance, with mixed weight transfer being a clever engineering contribution
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including multiple metrics, two diverse domains, ablation studies, and real2sim policy evaluation
Clear presentation with good intuitive figures (Figures 1-3) explaining the transformation pipeline
Thorough implementation details and hyperparameter documentation supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—mostly combines existing techniques (diffusion forcing [8], classifier-free guidance [27], causal masking) with incremental new contributions (mixed weight transfer, action dropout)
Single base model (DynamiCrafter 1.1B) evaluated; acknowledged computational constraints prevent testing on larger models (Sora, Veo-2), limiting evidence of generalization
Weak baseline comparisons—all baselines adapted from same base model; no comparison with AVID [43] or other recent world modeling approaches
Insufficient generalization analysis—limited to specific datasets (RT-1 manipulation tasks, CS:GO Dust II map); no cross-domain evaluation

Incomplete design justification—action guidance hyperparameters (scale 2.5, rescale 0.7) appear manually tuned; mixed weight transfer uses mean aggregation without justification or comparison to alternatives
Limited downstream task evaluation—Real2Sim uses only one task with small sample (N=80), requires human verification (not scalable), no inference efficiency analysis
Lack of systematic analysis of failure modes beyond Figure 6; no discussion of stochasticity in generated sequences; missing investigation of when causal generation degrades performance
Missing thorough ablation studies on action dropout rate sensitivity and action guidance scale effectiveness; no systematic exploration of design choices
No runtime or efficiency comparison with baselines despite acknowledgment that training is 'time-consuming'
Evaluation heavily relies on pixel-level metrics (FVD, FID); limited assessment of semantic understanding, physics consistency, or long-horizon prediction quality

strengths: Novel problem formulation leveraging internet-scale video data through pre-trained diffusion models for world modeling
Principled approach to temporal convolution causalization using extrapolative weight transfer with theoretical error bounds
Comprehensive multi-domain experimental evaluation (RT-1, CS:GO, RECON) demonstrating significant improvements over baselines
Strong practical results with Real2Sim policy evaluation showing the method enables downstream decision-making tasks
High reproducibility with detailed algorithms, implementation details, and hyperparameter specifications
Clear presentation and well-motivated problem statement with effective use of figures and visualizations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (causal masking, MLP action injection, classifier-free guidance); incremental contribution over prior work
Unfair baseline comparisons: most baselines are non-autoregressive and not designed for interactive generation, making the comparison with autoregressive Vid2World problematic
Theoretical gaps in extrapolative weight transfer: error bounds are loose (depend on uncharacterized smoothness constant L), linear approximation assumption not empirically validated

Incomplete experimental analysis: ablations use 30k steps vs 100k for main results limiting validity; missing sensitivity analyses for guidance scale and dropout rate; limited real2sim evaluation (50 trajectories, one task)
Limited model scale: 1.1B parameters is relatively lightweight; unclear how much improvement scaling provides and whether 'highly capable' characterization is justified
Insufficient failure mode analysis: acknowledges issues (fine-grained control, mode collapse) but provides limited investigation into when/why causalization or action conditioning fails
Limited evaluation scope: all domains are constrained closed-loop environments with short horizons (16 frames); no evaluation on open-ended scenarios or high-dimensional action spaces
Unjustified design choices: fixed guidance scale (2.5) across domains; p=2 for weight transfer with no sensitivity analysis; limited exploration of design space

strengths: Well-motivated problem: leveraging internet-scale action-free video data for world modeling is practically important
Systematic exploration of three weight transfer mechanisms with theoretical error bounds for the most principled approach
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three diverse domains (robot manipulation, game simulation, navigation) with multiple metrics
Strong quantitative results with substantial improvements over baselines (e.g., 79.9% FID improvement on CS:GO)
Proper ablation study demonstrating contribution of weight transfer mechanisms and action guidance
Good reproducibility: extensive implementation details, public base model, detailed hyperparameters
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines existing techniques (Diffusion Forcing, classifier-free guidance, action embeddings) without fundamental new insights; unclear what's novel vs. prior work (especially Chen et al., 2024)
Weight transfer mechanism lacks strong justification: linear extrapolation assumption for learned features is unjustified; no empirical validation of L-smoothness; no ablation on window size p

Action conditioning evaluation insufficient: modest gains in Table 2; no sensitivity analysis of guidance scale λ; no rigorous validation of claimed 'counterfactual reasoning' beyond showing different actions produce different outputs

Experimental methodology concerns: unfair baseline comparisons (both use same pre-trained base model but training time presented differently); limited downstream evaluation (only one small-scale Real2Sim experiment); metric inconsistencies across domains; no statistical significance testing
Scalability unclear: ~7 days training on 4×A100 GPUs not cheaper than baselines; only 1.1B model tested; authors acknowledge limitation to 'lightweight' models; no inference time analysis
Failure analysis weak: two categories mentioned but no systematic characterization of when/why failures occur or how to mitigate them

Missing rigorous evaluations: no sensitivity to key hyperparameters (λ, p, dropout rate); no long-horizon error analysis; no comparison to other foundation models beyond DIAMOND/NWM; claims about downstream decision-making support not well-validated

Architectural choices unjustified: why simple embedding addition for actions vs. cross-attention/FiLM? No ablation comparing action injection methods; limited analysis of interaction between diffusion forcing and action conditioning

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: Systematically leverages internet-scale action-free video data through pre-trained diffusion models to create interactive world models, addressing a practical bottleneck in world modeling research
Principled technical approach with theoretical grounding: Extrapolative Weight Transfer is well-justified with rigorous error analysis (Proposition 1) and counter-examples motivating the design

Comprehensive evaluation across diverse domains: Three distinct environments (robot manipulation, 3D gaming, open-world navigation) with multiple evaluation metrics (FVD, FID, SSIM, LPIPS, PSNR, DreamSim), proper ablations, and downstream task validation

Strong and consistent empirical results: Significant improvements across domains (71.1% FVD gain on CS:GO, 79.9% FID gain), with Real2Sim policy evaluation demonstrating practical utility beyond video generation metrics
Excellent execution and reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters, pseudocode algorithms, extensive appendices, and rigorous experimental methodology enabling reproduction
Practical significance: Avoids prohibitive cost of pre-training on massive corpora; leverages existing off-the-shelf models with minimal domain-specific fine-tuning across diverse environments
Clear presentation: Well-structured narrative with effective visual communication (data pyramid, challenge progression, solution architecture) and honest discussion of failure modes
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in individual components: Causal attention masking is straightforward, classifier-free guidance is established (Ho & Salimans 2022), and Diffusion Forcing is from Chen et al. (2024); contributions are more in systematic combination than fundamental algorithmic innovation

Generality claims undermined by single base model: Evaluation only on DynamiCrafter 1.1B without experiments on other pre-trained video diffusion models; limits ability to support broad applicability claims across video diffusion architectures

Incomplete causalization analysis: No direct ablation isolating the performance cost of enforcing causality; temporal generalization (training horizon 16 vs. testing 20 on RECON) is noted but not systematically analyzed

Insufficient hyperparameter analysis: Action guidance scale (λ=2.5), rescale factor (0.7), and dropout probability (p=0.2) are fixed across all domains without systematic sensitivity studies despite authors acknowledging domain-dependence
Limited downstream evaluation: Real2Sim policy evaluation uses only single task (drawer closing), small sample (N=50), human-only verification, and no ground truth real-world validation
Failure modes under-analyzed: Figure 8 shows failure cases (fine-grained control, object hallucination) but lacks quantitative analysis of failure types, frequencies, or systematic categorization

Missing critical analyses: No inference time/computational cost discussion (important for interactive applications), quantitative error accumulation curves, or systematic study of base model scale effects

Model scale and recency limitations: Using 1.1B parameter model while acknowledging larger SOTA models exist (NVIDIA Cosmos, Open-Sora 2.0); potentially limits practical impact and performance ceiling
